meta.title: Who really said "We are born crying, live complaining, and die disappointed"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: A line long attributed to Thomas Fuller and cited to his Gnomologia (1732), though its exact placement there is unconfirmed. It's the physician-aphorist Fuller (1654–1734), not the church historian, and it's often misattributed to Samuel Johnson.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We are born crying, live complaining, and die disappointed'?
meta.ogDescription: Long credited to Thomas Fuller and cited to his 1732 collection Gnomologia — by the physician Fuller (1654–1734), not the historian. Often wrongly pinned on Samuel Johnson.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1654–1734 · English physician & aphorist; compiler of ‘Gnomologia’ (1732). Not the church historian Thomas Fuller (1608–1661), with whom he is routinely confused.
answer.sourceLine: The line is long credited to Thomas Fuller and cited to his Gnomologia: Adagies and Proverbs (London, 1732) at p. 236 by Wikiquote — but in the full text it sits in an unnumbered appendix tagged ‘(The Optimist)’ rather than among the numbered proverbs, so its exact placement in Gnomologia is unconfirmed. Either way it is the physician Fuller (1654–1734), not the 1608 historian the quote sites credit.

author.name: Thomas Fuller
author.heading: About Thomas Fuller
author.metaLine: 1654–1734 · English physician & aphorist; compiler of Gnomologia (1732)
author.bio: Thomas Fuller (1654–1734) was an English physician, preacher and writer, best remembered today for Gnomologia (1732), a vast collection of proverbs, maxims and witty sayings later mined by Benjamin Franklin for Poor Richard’s Almanack. He is constantly confused with the far more famous Thomas Fuller (1608–1661), the church historian who wrote The Worthies of England and Good Thoughts in Bad Times — a mix-up that quote databases repeat wholesale.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on instead
misattribution.intro: The line is real and the attribution to “Thomas Fuller” is broadly correct — but two things go wrong almost every time it’s quoted.

items.why: Quote sites file it under the famous historian — e.g. Goodreads lists it beside Good Thoughts in Bad Times, and Wikiquote even places the Gnomologia (1732) citation under the 1608 clergyman. Gnomologia was compiled by the other Thomas Fuller, the physician (1654–1734), who was seven years old when the historian died.

A reworded version — “Man alone is born crying, lives complaining, and dies disappointed” — circulates widely under Samuel Johnson’s name, but with no primary source in Johnson’s essays, letters or Boswell’s Life. It reads as a later paraphrase of Fuller’s proverb.

misattribution.truthLine: The documented origin is Thomas Fuller’s Gnomologia (1732) — the physician-aphorist Fuller, not the historian, and not Samuel Johnson.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The proverb compresses a whole life into three sour beats — entrance, duration, exit — and the parallel grammar (born…live…die) makes it stick. That neat, epigrammatic shape is exactly what Fuller’s Gnomologia was built to preserve: over six thousand numbered sayings, harvested from classical, Continental and English sources for readers to quote.

Because Fuller was a collector, the line may well be older than any printing — and while it is long credited to him and cited to Gnomologia (1732), the full text segregates it in an unnumbered ‘(The Optimist)’ appendix rather than among the numbered proverbs, which is why we mark it ‘attributed’ rather than claiming Fuller coined it.
context.pull: Born crying, living complaining, dying disappointed — a life in three verbs.
